hub.name: From the Moon to the time on your clock

questions.prompt: Which object is between the Sun and Earth during a solar eclipse?
questions.explanation: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, blocking some or all of the Sun from a particular place.

questions.prompt: Which phase is needed for a lunar eclipse?
questions.explanation: Lunar eclipses happen at full Moon, when Earth can lie between the Sun and Moon. Most full Moons are not eclipsed.

questions.prompt: Why do eclipses not happen at every new and full Moon?
options: The Moon’s orbit is tilted, so the alignment usually misses
questions.explanation: The Moon’s tilted orbit usually carries it above or below the alignment needed for an eclipse.

title: Solar eclipse vs lunar eclipse: who is in the middle?

practice: Keep exploring the natural world with a few questions in Science Quiz.

sections.html:
In a solar eclipse, the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth. In a lunar eclipse, Earth passes between the Sun and Moon. The difference is who blocks the sunlight—and where the shadow falls.

Think of three objects lined up for a shadow show. Move the middle one and the story changes. The word solar points to the Sun; lunar points to the Moon.
sections.title: Same cast, different object in the middle

sections.html:
During a solar eclipse, the Moon can cover some or all of the Sun’s face from a particular place on Earth. The line-up is Sun → Moon → Earth, at new Moon.

During a lunar eclipse, the Moon moves into Earth’s shadow. The line-up is Sun → Earth → Moon, at full Moon. NASA’s eclipse guide explains both arrangements.

A totally eclipsed Moon can look reddish. Some sunlight reaches it after travelling through Earth’s atmosphere, which scatters more of the blue light. The Moon has not switched on a red lamp.
sections.title: One hides the Sun; the other dims the Moon

sections.html:
New Moons and full Moons each return roughly once a month, so why not two eclipses?

The Moon’s orbit is tilted relative to Earth’s path around the Sun. Most months, the alignment misses: the Moon passes above or below the Sun in our sky, or above or below Earth’s shadow. NASA explains this geometry.

That is also why ordinary Moon phases are not little eclipses. Phases come from our changing view of the Moon’s sunlit half.
sections.title: Why is there no eclipse every month?

sections.html:
Ask: “What is in the middle?” Moon in the middle: solar eclipse. Earth in the middle: lunar eclipse. You do not need a calendar of eclipse dates to understand the difference.

You can explore shadows with a lamp and a ball indoors. Do not use the Sun for this experiment. If you plan to watch a solar eclipse, follow NASA’s viewing-safety guidance; ordinary sunglasses are not safe solar viewers.
sections.title: A small trick for remembering

description: The Sun, Earth and Moon can make two very different shadow shows. Discover which object moves between the others, and why it does not happen every month.
